corridor.grand_canal.title: Grand Canal of Beijing
corridor.grand_canal.intro: The principal field laboratory. Imperial history, water infrastructure, urban transformation, food and agricultural flows, trade, and heritage policy converge in Beijing's canal landscape.
corridor.grand_canal.detail: The Grand Canal is a UNESCO World Heritage site (Reference C 1443, inscribed 2014), described not only as an engineering and transportation achievement but also in terms of political and economic unification, cultural interchange, and distinctive ways of life along its course. The Beijing section functions as a deep field laboratory within the larger canal system, with particular attention to the subtle interfaces between the Grand Canal and wider Silk Roads systems of movement and exchange. Evidence: UNWTO/Silk Road Programme; UNESCO WHC C 1443 [A]; drafted research proposal [B].
corridor.gotland.title: Gotland
corridor.gotland.intro: The principal Swedish comparison — a Baltic island whose Viking Age and Hanseatic past demonstrates intense long-distance connectivity alongside a strong local cultural identity.
corridor.gotland.detail: Gotland provides a genuine conceptual comparison to Beijing: how can a place participate intensely in distant networks while retaining a strong local cultural identity? Archaeological work at Viking Age Ridanäs (Fröjel) demonstrates substantial long-distance connectivity, with imported materials from mainland Sweden, Italy, Poland/Lithuania and the Caucasus (Carlsson 1999; Peschel et al. 2017), while isotope evidence indicates approximately 85% of studied individuals were local (Peschel et al. 2017, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 13: 175-184). Visby, the main Hanseatic centre in the Baltic from the 12th to 14th century, is a UNESCO World Heritage site (Reference 731, 1995). Evidence: UNESCO WHC 731 [A]; Peschel et al. 2017 [A]; drafted research proposal [B].
corridor.southern_oland.title: Southern Öland
corridor.southern_oland.intro: A focused regeneration laboratory — UNESCO-listed agricultural landscape where archaeological soil and food are used to explore how the past generates future life.
corridor.southern_oland.detail: Southern Öland is inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site (Agricultural Landscape of Southern Öland, Reference 968, 2000). Recent excavations at Gamla Skogsby (2019-ongoing), led by Ludvig Papmehl-Dufay (Linnaeus University), have revealed an Iron Age chieftain's estate with 19 house foundations, extensive food-preparation evidence, and pig-bone assemblages associated with feasting (Papmehl-Dufay 2020-2025). Cornelius Holtorf's published chapter 'An Archaeology of Growth and Regeneration' (2022) explicitly connects this archaeological food and soil evidence to the idea of the past generating future life. Evidence: UNESCO WHC 968 [A]; Papmehl-Dufay 2020-2025 [A]; Holtorf 2022 [A].
corridor.linkoping.title: Linköping / Kinda Canal
corridor.linkoping.intro: An auxiliary infrastructure comparison — what happens to cultural meaning when an infrastructure loses its original economic function.
corridor.linkoping.detail: The Kinda Canal was completed in 1871 and historically connected southern forest-producing areas with northern agricultural areas, supporting commerce and communication before later transport technologies displaced much of its original role. It now survives partly through cultural and tourism functions and is designated a 'kulturhistoriskt värdefull miljö av riksintresse' (culturally valuable environment of national interest). The Kinda Canal connects to the broader Göta Canal system via Lake Roxen (Nykvarn lock), linking local/regional and national/international waterway networks. Evidence: Linköpings kommun; kindakanal.se [B]; drafted research proposal [B].
